document.description: CheW is a small (167 aa) soluble cytoplasmic coupling protein of the Escherichia coli chemotaxis system, composed of a single CheW-like domain of two SH3-like beta-barrel subdomains, homologous to the P5 domain of the histidine kinase CheA. CheW binds directly to the cytoplasmic hairpin tips of methyl-accepting chemoreceptors (Tar, Tsr, Trg, Tap, Aer) and to the P5 domain of CheA, physically linking the kinase to the receptors. Receptor trimers of dimers, CheW and CheA form ternary core signaling units (two receptor trimers, two CheW and one CheA dimer) that network into hexagonal arrays at the cell poles; CheW binding promotes receptor clustering and CheA recruitment. Within these arrays CheW is required for receptor-mediated activation and stimulus control of CheA autophosphorylation and thus of phosphotransfer to CheY and CheB, and cheW mutants swim smoothly and are non-chemotactic.

review.summary: IPI from Boukhvalova et al. 2002: purified CheW binds both CheA and the aspartate receptor Tar, and mutations abolishing either binding interaction abolish assembly of active ternary complexes and chemotaxis.
review.reason: Bare protein binding is uninformative. This paper shows that CheW binds both the kinase and the receptor and that each binding interaction is needed for an active receptor-CheW-CheA complex, which is exactly the molecular adaptor activity that defines CheW. Replace with GO:0030159 signaling receptor complex adaptor activity (the core MF of this review). The specific term describes physical support for assembly of a multiprotein receptor signaling complex, matching CheW bridging receptor tips to CheA.

supported_by.supporting_text: Our results indicate that mutations which eliminate CheW binding to Tar (V36M) or to CheA (G57D) result in a complete inability to form active ternary complexes in vitro and render the CheW protein incapable of mediating chemotaxis in vivo.

Receptor directly bound CheW, but receptor-CheA binding was dependent upon the presence of CheW. These observations in combination with our previous identification of a CheW-CheA complex suggest that CheW physically links the kinase to the receptor.

document.title: Bacterial chemotaxis signal transduction to flagellar motor output
document.description: Bacterial chemoreceptor-to-flagellar-motor signaling through receptor-coupled CheA phosphotransfer and a motor-output CheY receiver. Membrane and cytoplasmic receptor architectures, CheW/CheV coupling, lineage-dependent motor responses and optional receptor-adaptation/reset mechanisms are represented separately. The model includes Bacillus CheC/CheD and FliY mechanisms, divergent Helicobacter CheZ/ChePep organization, and Sinorhizobium phosphate drainage. Taxon scope describes the reusable bacterial mechanism, not universal occurrence or equivalent native kinetics. Sodium-conducting PomAB and coexisting CheX/CheZ reset exemplars extend the mechanistic scope.

evidence.statement: Canonical E. coli architecture does not define all bacterial chemotaxis systems.
evidence.supporting_text: Here, we compare the canonical chemotaxis system of E. coli with systems that diverge in supramolecular architecture, sensory mechanisms, and protein composition.

evidence.statement: Some bacteria assemble multiple arrays with different sensory coverage and localization.

evidence.title: Altering chemotaxis as a strategy to enhance the foraging range of motility-restricted bacteria.
evidence.statement: CheX and CheZ can coexist and make distinct contributions to chemotaxis in the same bacterial system.
evidence.supporting_text: CheX and CheZ jointly regulate but exert distinct effects on V. vulnificus chemotaxis.

document.notes: The original E. coli/Pseudomonas pathway has been expanded with experimentally differentiated bacterial implementations. Basal receiver turnover and optional acceleration are separated; optionality denotes the broad machinery model and does not imply normal behavior after deleting a native component. CheR/CheB, CheC/CheD and CheV feedback can coexist. CheS is not asserted to be a phosphatase or direct CheA-CheY1 bridge, and CheT acts on sink CheY1-P rather than motor CheY2-P. Whole receiver families are not equated to motor-output CheY. Complex active units require conjunctive evaluation by the external oracle; the production compiler treats each complex annoton as an atom. Wsp, Chp, alternative cellular-function outputs and flagellar construction/export are outside this signaling model. Sodium PomAB and coexisting CheX/CheZ implementations are integrated. Final production-compiler/oracle checks, focused module validation and full-corpus validation remain pending.

title: Bacterial chemotaxis signal transduction to flagellar motor output
description: Bacterial chemoreceptor-to-flagellar-motor signaling through receptor-coupled CheA phosphotransfer
  and a motor-output CheY receiver. Membrane and cytoplasmic receptor architectures, CheW/CheV coupling,
  lineage-dependent motor responses and optional receptor-adaptation/reset mechanisms are represented
  separately. The model includes Bacillus CheC/CheD and FliY mechanisms, divergent Helicobacter CheZ/ChePep
  organization, and Sinorhizobium phosphate drainage. Taxon scope describes the reusable bacterial mechanism,
  not universal occurrence or equivalent native kinetics. Sodium-conducting PomAB and coexisting CheX/CheZ
  reset exemplars extend the mechanistic scope.

# cheW (E. coli K-12, UniProt P0A964) review notes

## 2026-11-03 session

Deep research: `just deep-research ECOLI cheW --provider perplexity` failed ("Provider 'perplexity' not
available."). `just mod-description-deep-research ECOLI cheW`
skipped ("no MOD provider configured for organism 'ECOLI'"). Review based on cached publications
(most abstract-only; PMID:19547746 and PMID:25060668 full text) and the UniProt record.

Literature search: PubMed esearch queries via eutils for CheW/CheA/chemoreceptor array, CheW polar
localization; no additional PMIDs were needed beyond the GOA set.

### Key evidence
- CheW is the receptor-kinase coupling adaptor: [PMID:1326408 "Receptor directly bound CheW, but receptor-CheA binding was dependent upon the presence of CheW. These observations in combination with our previous identification of a CheW-CheA complex suggest that CheW physically links the kinase to the receptor."]
- Both binding arms are needed: [PMID:11923283 "mutations which eliminate CheW binding to Tar (V36M) or to CheA (G57D) result in a complete inability to form active ternary complexes in vitro and render the CheW protein incapable of mediating chemotaxis in vivo"]
- CheW-CheA binding: [PMID:1992467 "CheW and CheA exhibit reversible binding with the stoichiometry of two CheW monomers per CheA dimer."]
- Core unit stoichiometry: [PMID:21606342 "Purified complexes contained two receptor trimers of dimers and two CheW for each CheA dimer"]
- Receptor-dependent clustering at poles: [PMID:19547746 "Clustering of labeled CheW requires receptors since deletion of high-abundance chemotaxis receptors abrogated clustering of CheW (Figure 3H)."]
- Soluble pool: [PMID:334749 "the cheY, cheW, and cheA (66,000 daltons) polypeptides appeared only in the soluble cytoplasmic fraction"]
- Genetics: [PMID:353036 "Mutants defective in cheA, cheW, cheX, or cheY function swam smoothly, with little or no tumbling"]

### Decisions (27 rows)
